**Chapter Nine: Acid-Base Balance**

**Most of fruits slightly acidic.**

We use various kinds of compounds in a chemical laboratory. Acids, bases and salts are most frequently used. As chemistry learners, you also need to learn about acid, base and salt. We mostly use diluted acids and bases instead of concentrated acids or bases in our laboratories. We take in acids, bases and salts with our food which is important for our bodies. Salt is formed by neutralizing acid with base or vice versa. We can determine the acidity from various experiments in the laboratory. Litmus test and pH value test are the most commonly used. These necessary acids, bases and salts are also harmful to some extent to our environment. We will discuss about all these in this chapter.

**9.1 Introduction**

Acids, bases and salts are the most frequently used compounds in a chemical laboratory. As chemistry learners, you also need to learn about acid, base and salt. We mostly use diluted acids and bases instead of concentrated acids or bases in our laboratories. We take in acids, bases and salts with our food which is important for our bodies. Salt is formed by neutralizing acid with base or vice versa. We can determine the acidity from various experiments in the laboratory. Litmus test and pH value test are the most commonly used. These necessary acids, bases and salts are also harmful to some extent to our environment. We will discuss about all these in this chapter.

**9.2 Acids**

Acids are substances that donate a proton (H+ ion) in a solution. They have a pH less than 7. There are two types of acids: strong acids and weak acids. Strong acids completely dissociate in water, while weak acids only partially dissociate. Examples of strong acids include hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), and nitric acid (HNO3). Examples of weak acids include acetic acid (CH3COOH), citric acid (C6H8O7), and ascorbic acid (C6H8O6).

**9.3 Bases**

Bases are substances that accept a proton (H+ ion) in a solution. They have a pH greater than 7. There are two types of bases: strong bases and weak bases. Strong bases completely dissociate in water, while weak bases only partially dissociate. Examples of strong bases include sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH), and calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2). Examples of weak bases include ammonia (NH3), methylamine (CH3NH2), and ethylamine (C2H5NH2).

**9.4 Salts**

Salts are formed by the reaction of an acid and a base. They are neutral substances that do not have a pH less than 7 or greater than 7. Examples of salts include sodium chloride (NaCl), potassium nitrate (KNO3), and calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

**9.5 Litmus Test**

The litmus test is a simple test used to determine if a substance is an acid or a base. Litmus is a mixture of two dyes, one red and one blue. When litmus is added to an acid, it turns red. When litmus is added to a base, it turns blue.

**9.6 pH Value Test**

The pH value test is a more accurate test used to determine the pH of a substance. pH stands for "potential of hydrogen" and is a measure of the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution. A pH of 7 is neutral, while a pH less than 7 is acidic and a pH greater than 7 is basic.

**9.7 Conclusion**
